noticias.titulo: Trump calls to ‘expedite’ US federal executions, blasts Gavin Newsom
noticias.resumen: The US president used his podium to attack the California governor for a decision to commute 548 death sentences.
noticias.texto:
Trump calls to ‘expedite’ US federal executions, blasts Gavin Newsom
The US president used his podium to attack the California governor for a decision to commute 548 death sentences.
United States President Donald Trump has reaffirmed his support for the death penalty in an event that doubled as a platform to attack one of his most visible critics, California Governor Gavin Newsom.
On Monday, Trump spoke at the Department of Justice in Washington, DC, where he was joined by the families of crime victims and his attorney general, Todd Blanche.
“The ultimate crimes deserve the ultimate punishment,” Trump said of the death penalty, calling it a cornerstone of “ virtually every society throughout history, at least every successful society”.
“Under the Trump administration, we are bringing it back, and we will not stop in our pursuit of justice. We will not yield.”
He concluded the appearance by signing a presidential directive ordering the Department of Justice to seek the death penalty in murder cases involving children, rape and human trafficking.
The directive also pushes for the attorney general to “expedite” executions for those on federal death row.
As part of his speech, Trump called on Congress to pass the Just Punishment for Murder Act, a bill sponsored by Republican Representative Brandon Gill, which the president said would “strengthen the death penalty in America”.
But he dedicated much of his remarks to slamming Newsom, a Democrat widely seen as a possible contender for the 2028 presidential race.
Newsom’s second term as governor will end on January 4. Under California term limits, he was ineligible to run again in the 2026 midterm elections.
Still, the governor and former San Francisco mayor has carved a national profile for himself as a proxy for Democrats during high-stakes political campaigns — and as a critic of Trump.
Trump, however, zeroed in on one of Newsom’s final major actions while in office: commuting the sentences of those on California’s death row.
On November 5, two days after the midterms, Newsom announced that the 548 people sentenced to death in California would instead be sentenced to life without the possibility of parole.
He described the action as an extension of the moratorium on executions he put in place after taking office in 2019.
“I could not remain true to my values and oversee the killing of people with death warrants in California,” he wrote in an open letter.
He nevertheless denounced the harm the 548 people had caused.
“Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die,” Newsom wrote. “But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them.”
He called on Californians to let the 548 people “die in obscurity” while remembering their victims.
Trump, however, framed the mass commutation as an effort to help “evil monsters” escape justice.
“This afternoon, we come together to stand against the travesty and to wrap our arms around the families of victims who were so cruelly betrayed by bad government and our political system,” Trump said.
The president proceeded to launch barbs at Newsom, calling him “ a terrible governor” who “ stole away the only closure” the victims’ families “might ever have”.
He then invited several family members on stage to denounce Newsom’s decision.
“ You took the only justice we had and left families feeling abandoned by the state that promised to protect us,” Sandra Friend, the mother of eight-year-old murder victim Michael Lyons, said in her remarks, directed at Newsom.
In anticipation of Monday’s news conference, Newsom also released statements from families that supported his choice.
“When victims are this divided, the death penalty shouldn’t be the answer. Victims deserve so much more than a promise of justice through vengeance,” Jess Nichol, the sister of murder victim Polly Klaas, said in one of the statements.
“They deserve counselling, medical care, financial support, and a justice system that helps them heal. I want something better for survivors: real, tangible support.”
The tit-for-tat between Newsom and Trump comes as support for the death penalty has slumped in recent years.
A November poll released by the research firm Gallup found that 49 percent of US adults support the death penalty, the lowest rate since 1971.
Opponents of the death penalty have frequently pointed to the prevalence of botched executions and the possibility that innocent people may be executed.
The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit, has found that approximately 202 people formerly on death row were later found to be wrongfully convicted. The exoneration rate, it said, was one for every eight people executed in the US.
Death penalty cases also typically tend to result in longer court battles and higher costs.
Before Newsom’s mass commutation, California reportedly had the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere, representing roughly a quarter of the country’s death sentences.
Newsom’s successor, Governor-elect Xavier Becerra, has pledged to continue the death penalty moratorium once sworn in.
But that policy puts California at odds with a push under Trump to embrace the death penalty and expand execution methods.
Upon taking office for a second term on January 20, 2025, Trump signed the first of several executive orders aimed at “restoring the death penalty”.
He pushed to have execution be the de facto punishment for the murder of law enforcement officers, as well as for murder cases where undocumented immigrants are the defendants.
In April, the Trump administration also said it would prioritise the use of the death penalty by expanding the acceptable methods for federal execution, including firing squads.
In October, Trump’s Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that one execution by firing squad — that of the Fort Hood shooter, Nidal Hasan — would be livestreamed to the public, prompting backlash.
Trump later walked back the announcement, amid reports that he did not realise Hassan was in a wheelchair.
During his first term, Trump oversaw 13 federal executions, the most of any president in decades. In Monday’s speech, he framed such punishments as “common sense”.
“ When it comes to defending the lives and safety of American people, there can be no compromise,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Borno school enrolment nearly doubles after years of conflict
noticias.resumen: Despite rising enrolment, violence, displacement and poverty keep children out of school in northeastern state.
noticias.texto:
Borno school enrolment nearly doubles after years of conflict
Despite rising enrolment, violence, displacement and poverty keep children out of school in northeastern state.
Maiduguri, Nigeria – During years of Boko Haram violence, Maryam Umar’s school in Baga, a town in northeastern Nigeria’s Borno State, was forced to close as violence displaced families and disrupted education across the region.
The closure of the Higher Islamic College in Baga in the Kukawa Local Government Area was part of a wider crisis that deprived thousands of children of regular schooling.
With educational activities now resuming, Umar, a teacher, welcomed efforts to reopen schools and provide learning materials, telling Al Jazeera that the interventions were helping restore education in communities devastated by years of conflict.
Across Borno, authorities said school enrolment has risen sharply as damaged classrooms are repaired and families are encouraged to send their children back to school.
Enrolment in public and private schools reached 1,418,279 learners in 2025, up from 766,551 during the 2017-2018 academic session, according to the state government.
Yet officials estimated that almost 800,000 children remain out of school, highlighting the challenges facing a state where more than a decade of conflict has displaced communities and devastated public services.
The figures suggest progress in expanding access but reveal little about regular attendance, teaching quality or whether children who have missed years of education are catching up.
Rebuilding after years of violence
Borno has been at the centre of Boko Haram violence since the armed group launched its campaign in northeastern Nigeria in 2009.
Schools were among the institutions affected as attacks, displacement and a prolonged lack of security forced families to abandon their homes. In some communities, education became impossible as classrooms closed and teachers and pupils fled.
The state government has made school reconstruction a priority, building new facilities and rehabilitating classrooms damaged by conflict and flooding.
“In response, our administration has constructed 104 new schools and rehabilitated 2,931 classrooms and related facilities,” Governor Babagana Umara Zulum said during the commissioning of educational projects in Maiduguri in March.
According to the governor, the estimated number of out-of-school children has fallen from about 2.2 million at the height of the crisis to fewer than 800,000.
Borno Commissioner for Education, Science, Technology and Innovation Lawan Abba Wakilbe said the increase in enrolment reflects renewed confidence among parents.
But increased enrolment does not necessarily mean children are attending regularly or receiving the support they need after years of disrupted learning.
The available figures also provide little indication of whether the supply of qualified teachers and learning materials has kept pace with the growing number of pupils.
A generation returning to classrooms
For 12-year-old Fatima Mahmud Umar, a student at the Junior Secondary School One in Maiduguri, education offers an opportunity to pursue ambitions that years of violence have threatened for children across Borno.
Wearing a blue and white chequered hijab and her school uniform, Fatima spoke to Al Jazeera about her hopes for the future.
She expressed gratitude to her parents for supporting her education and said she hopes to become a good ambassador for her community.
Fatima also welcomed government investment in schools, including efforts to support both Islamic and Western education.
But many children across Borno have yet to regain access to regular schooling.
Violence, displacement and poverty continue to create obstacles, particularly for families struggling to rebuild their lives after years of upheaval.
Even where schools have reopened, children who missed months or years of lessons may struggle to catch up with their peers while teachers must accommodate pupils with widely different levels of preparation.
For returning students, enrolment is only the first step. Their prospects also depend on whether schools can provide the support needed to help them progress.
Rural communities left behind
The challenge is particularly pressing in rural communities, where distance, violence and limited resources can make regular schooling difficult.
In the Gubio Local Government Area, residents have raised concerns about children who remain outside formal education despite the government’s reconstruction efforts.
Bukar Abdullahi, 49, highlighted the need to enrol more children during a town hall meeting in Gubio.
While commending the state government for investing in education, Abdullahi drew attention to the difficulties facing rural communities.
For families living far from functioning schools, distance can remain an obstacle. Financial pressures and concerns about safety may also affect decisions about whether children attend.
Although the government’s figures suggest improved access, they do not show how evenly progress is distributed between urban centres and rural communities.
Addressing those disparities will require more than classrooms. Schools also need qualified teachers, learning materials and measures to help families keep their children enrolled.
Expanding Islamic education
Alongside conventional schools, Borno authorities are seeking to widen educational opportunities through Arabic and Islamic institutions.
Through the Borno State Arabic and Sangaya Education Board, the government is working to integrate aspects of traditional Islamic learning into a system offering recognised qualifications and pathways to further study.
The establishment of Higher Islamic Colleges is part of that effort.
“This intervention reflects our commitment to building an inclusive education system that integrates spiritual development with academic and vocational advancement,” Zulum said.
According to the governor, the institutions follow a curriculum approved by the National Board for Arabic and Islamic Studies that allows students to pursue recognised qualifications.
The initiative aims to expand opportunities for children whose families favour Islamic education, but its impact will depend on whether institutions can reach underserved communities and provide adequate teaching and resources.
Beyond enrolment figures
More recent government statistics indicate further expansion of Borno’s education system although differences in the categories counted make direct comparisons difficult.
The state’s annual school census, released in September, recorded 1,801,295 learners across the wider education sector.
Separately, enrolment in public primary and secondary schools stood at about 1.3 million during the 2025-2026 academic session.
Those figures cover different categories from the 1,418,279 learners recorded across public and private schools in 2025 and cannot be directly compared to establish the precise rate of growth.
The government’s estimate that nearly 800,000 children remain out of school also requires context. Without consistent information on the age groups and methodology used, the reported decline from 2.2 million cannot be independently assessed from the figures provided.
Beyond enrolment, questions remain about attendance, teacher availability and learning outcomes, particularly for children whose education was interrupted by conflict.
For teachers such as Umar in Baga, the resumption of educational activities marks a change from the years when violence forced schools to close. For children such as Fatima in Maiduguri, access to education offers opportunities that years of violence have threatened to take away.
But for the hundreds of thousands still outside classrooms, Borno’s educational recovery remains unfinished.
For Wakilbe, the increase in enrolment is nevertheless a sign that families are beginning to regain confidence in the education system.
“When you look at where we started, 766,551 learners in 2017-2018, and see where we are today, this is not just a number. It is evidence that parents and communities once again trust our schools with their children’s future,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Drone attack on Colombia police base injures civilians, including infant
noticias.resumen: Far-right President De la Espriella steps up offensive as rebel groups strike back with drone strikes, roadside bombs.
noticias.texto:
Drone attack on Colombia police base injures civilians, including infant
Far-right President De la Espriella steps up offensive as rebel groups strike back with drone strikes, roadside bombs.
A drone attack on a police base in the Colombian city of Cucuta has injured at least three civilians, including an infant, and damaged 60 homes.
Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on Monday that struck the base belonging to the Norte de Santander police.
Orlando Roa, who lives near the base, told local media that his 18-month-old grandson was among those injured and was being treated at a nearby hospital.
The attack came as far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up an offensive against rebel groups and drug gangs that has resulted in the military capturing several mid-level commanders.
Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, who took office in August, has cancelled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were under way under his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro.
Cucuta, a city near Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and a centre for criminal groups profiting from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling. Rebel groups, including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC, also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region.
In 2016, a peace deal between the Colombian government and the FARC led to the demobilisation of more than 14,000 fighters.
However, some border areas in Colombia have seen a surge of violence as smaller armed groups try to seize territory abandoned by the FARC, where the government has been slow to provide security and basic services.
Another police station in the Cesar region was also attacked with drones on Monday, injuring a police officer. On Saturday, one soldier was killed, and 12 others were injured during an attack with drones and rockets on a military base also in Cesar.
Both incidents remain under investigation, according to local officials.

noticias.titulo: EU plans sports ban in sweeping new Russia sanctions proposal
noticias.resumen: Proposed sanctions aim to curb Russian crypto financing and 'propaganda' in sports.
noticias.texto:
EU plans sports ban in sweeping new Russia sanctions proposal
Proposed sanctions aim to curb Russian crypto financing and ‘propaganda’ in sports.
The European Commission has proposed new sanctions against Russia targeting its banks, crypto platforms, and participation in sporting events.
Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen introduced the 22nd package of sanctions on Monday, which includes a ban on Russian teams and individual athletes competing under the country’s flag at events in the European Union.
“We are striking harder at Russia’s ways to finance its war, by targeting its banks and crypto platforms,” von der Leyen wrote in a post on X, adding that the EU will be “shutting the door to its participation in European sports and cultural events”.
Economic pressure
Von der Leyen said 60 banks will be removed from the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) messaging system used for international payments under the new proposals, which are intended to maintain economic pressure on Russia, almost five years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
She announced the creation of a crypto sanctions task force seeking to curb countries helping Russia to evade sanctions.
The commission also proposed a ban on visas for Russians who had fought in the war in Ukraine.
“Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries,” von der Leyen said.
‘Propaganda activities’
The plan also put forward restrictions on financial flows from Russian sponsors to sports and cultural associations based in the EU. Russian nationals would also no longer be allowed to hold leadership positions on the governing bodies of sports federations.
“Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities,” said von der Leyen.
The proposed package must be endorsed by all 27 EU member countries before going into force and comes just over a month after the bloc posted the largest listing of sanctions against Russia, targeting about 1,600 Russian officials and companies linked to its arms industry.
The EU has already slapped sanctions on more than 4,200 people and entities, including Russian President Vladimir Putin and several energy companies.

noticias.titulo: What Nvidia’s Jensen Huang’s return means for Washington and Wall Street?
noticias.resumen: Trump claims credit for Huang's return, raising concerns over federal government meddling in corporate board decisions.
noticias.texto:
What Nvidia’s Jensen Huang’s return means for Washington and Wall Street?
Trump claims credit for Huang’s return, raising concerns over federal government meddling in corporate board decisions.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s dramatic return to the helm of the world’s most valuable chipmaker, less than two weeks after his resignation, has sent the company’s stock soaring.
At the same time, the White House’s involvement in his reinstatement has raised questions about Silicon Valley’s growing sway in Washington, with United States President Donald Trump claiming to have been a linchpin in the decision.
What happened?
The saga began less than two weeks ago when Huang resigned amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Beijing has denied that Alice Huang is a spy. She previously led Megaspeed, a company that had a business relationship with Nvidia, the Santa Clara, California-based tech giant.
Nvidia’s board had begun an investigation into the allegations, but Huang resigned before it reached a conclusion.
In his absence, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress took over as interim chief executive while the board searched for a permanent successor.
However, Huang’s departure quickly prompted a backlash from influential figures in Silicon Valley. A petition calling for his reinstatement attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including that of SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Analysts also warned that losing Huang could significantly undermine Nvidia’s market value. Dan Ives, managing partner at Yorkville Ives, estimated that Huang’s departure could wipe as much as 30 percent off the company’s valuation.
By Monday, Nvidia brought Huang back to lead the company.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C Jones, chair of the board, in a news statement. That was an about-face from just a few days ago when the board ruled out bringing back Huang.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” Huang added.
How has the Trump administration been involved?
Trump said on Monday that he played a central role in Huang’s reinstatement, saying in social media posts and in an interview with CNBC that his intervention had been instrumental in the board’s decision.
Trump said he had participated in the board meeting, following efforts by influential Silicon Valley figures to persuade the president to intervene in the leadership crisis, which analysts say lacked a clear succession plan.
Trump told CNBC that the stock market reaction to Huang’s resignation from Nvidia “probably” factored into his decision to push for the CEO’s reinstatement, although his view of the long-term benefit of having Huang at the helm of the company was the bigger weight, the Reuters news agency reported.
“I think this move is unprecedented in the sense that a sitting president has exerted very public pressure on a corporate board to make a particular decision,” Aleksandar Tomic, associate dean for strategy, innovation and technology at Boston College, told Al Jazeera.
Corporate governance experts say greater transparency is needed about the extent of Trump’s involvement in Nvidia’s leadership decisions.
“A board can take input from [the] government; what it should not do is let any outside party choose the CEO without explaining to shareholders why,” Martin Mulyadi, professor of accounting at Shenandoah University’s College of Business, Engineering & Technology, told Al Jazeera.
The intervention comes amid divisions within the Trump administration over Nvidia’s business practices and its relationship with China.
The Department of Justice (DOJ) and Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) continue to investigate the company, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has emerged as one of its most vocal critics.
Bessent has questioned whether Nvidia facilitated chip sales to China to bolster its financial performance, alleging in an interview with Fox News that the AI chip giant had engaged in “seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings”.
He has also called for Nvidia to appoint a new chief executive from outside the company.
Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces allegations that he delayed restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China, raising questions about whether his decisions were influenced by the financial interests of his former firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, which is now controlled by his two sons.
Democratic lawmakers are seeking to determine whether the firm’s holdings or business relationships benefitted from the Commerce Department’s failure to impose those restrictions.
“The key issue is how much of Nvidia’s revenue may be coming from sales that would not pass increased scrutiny vis-a-vis export control violations. Given accusations within the government of lax monitoring and enforcement, it is also not clear that Nvidia had robust controls, and their inability to stick to the CEO decision makes it doubtful that they will be able to implement it in the future,” Tomic said.
What precedent does the decision set?
Trump’s involvement has also raised broader questions about the relationship between the federal government and corporate America, particularly the extent to which a president should influence decisions traditionally reserved for a company’s board of directors.
Tomic says that the level of direct pressure Trump placed on Nvidia’s board, including his participation in discussions about Huang’s reinstatement, is highly unusual for a sitting president.
The precedent could ultimately backfire on Republicans, Tomic warned, particularly as Democrats prepare to take control of both the House and Senate in January. Democrats have historically pushed for greater oversight of large corporations, and the incoming Congress could seek to exercise similar influence over corporate decision-making.
“I think that Nvidia will invite much stronger government scrutiny, especially with Congress and the new administration in 2028, as they have shown a complete lack of capacity for self-governance,” Tomic said.
Nvidia’s board’s decision to reinstate Huang could have lasting implications for corporate accountability, particularly in Silicon Valley, where investors frequently place enormous value on the leadership of company founders, Tomic added.
Huang’s reinstatement could reinforce the perception that prominent technology executives are indispensable to their companies, potentially making it more difficult to hold them accountable for personal or professional misconduct, he said.
“It is hard to imagine any other industry where this would happen. The attitude of immunity and idolatry of tech founders is grating on voters and is one of the reasons for the electoral outcome. This is an unforced error, as Huang could have stayed substantially involved at Nvidia in a much less public way,” Tomic added.
How have markets reacted?
Wall Street welcomed the news of Huang’s return, sending Nvidia shares soaring approximately 31 percent in early trading on Monday. The stock maintained much of those gains throughout the session.
The rally extended beyond Nvidia, helping lift broader US stock markets, with all three major indices finishing the trading day in positive territory.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 rose nearly 7 percent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 3 percent and the S&P 500 climbed 4.7 percent.
Other major technology companies also benefitted from the rally. Shares of rival chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) jumped 6.85 percent, while Microsoft gained 1.65 percent and Alphabet rose 5.8 percent.
Why does this decision matter for the broader markets?
Nvidia has taken an outsized role in the broader markets. As of October, the tech giant accounted for 8.1 percent of the Nasdaq 100 index.
According to an analysis by The Wall Street Journal, Nvidia has amassed investments worth more than $100bn, including more than $48bn in shares of eight publicly traded companies, citing SEC filings.
Among those holdings is a 10 percent stake in CoreWeave, a cloud-computing company that operates data centres. CoreWeave shares surged 22 percent following news of Huang’s reinstatement.
Nvidia has broader connections to other companies.
In late August, Amazon announced plans to deploy an additional two million Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) through its cloud-computing division, Amazon Web Services, in 2027 and 2028. That commitment followed a previously announced deployment of more than one million GPUs in March.
Nvidia has also deepened its financial ties to Anthropic, committing $10bn to buy shares in the AI company’s blockbuster initial public offering on US markets late last week.

noticias.titulo: US escalates sanctions on Iran, targets ‘shadow banking’ networks
noticias.resumen: US Treasury sanctions over two dozen Iranian entities, citing efforts to disrupt Tehran's global financial activities.
noticias.texto:
US escalates sanctions on Iran, targets ‘shadow banking’ networks
US Treasury sanctions more than two dozen Iranian entities, citing efforts to disrupt Tehran’s global financial activities, amid ongoing diplomatic effort to end the US-Israel war on Iran.
The United States has launched another wave of sanctions against Iran under its Operation Economic Outcast, a move that comes shortly after US President Donald Trump threatened renewed military action next year.
The Department of the Treasury announced on Monday that it had targeted more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel with sanctions “in a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran’s global shadow banking networks”.
“Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime,” said US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent.
The US Treasury claimed these entities help Iran “move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions”.
Bessent also vowed the “Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake.”
The Central Bank of Iran oversees the designated entities, according to the statement.
The designated entities include an Iran-based company named “Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company (Nesim Baharan)”, which the Treasury claims worked closely with Iranian exchange houses and their front companies to facilitate transactions on behalf of Sarmayeh Bank’s Iranian clients, which include major Iranian petrochemical companies.
In addition, “Mina Fashki and Partners Exchange Company (Fashki Exchange) and Mellat Exchange Company” and a number of their owners and employees were designated.
The US claimed earlier this month that its sanctions campaign had pushed Iran’s rial to new lows and driven inflation to about 90 percent.
AP reported that Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran still hoped diplomacy could end its nine-month war with the US, while President Trump said Iran wanted a deal, but one that was not acceptable to him.
Fox News said Trump told its chief foreign correspondent that he was “inclined to order military strikes against Iran after the new year if the two countries fail to reach an agreement”.
The remarks came as diplomatic efforts continued to end a conflict that has destabilised the Middle East, disrupted shipping, driven up global energy prices, and drawn in countries across the region.

noticias.texto:
US states sue SpaceX over Grok AI’s creation of child sexual abuse material
Virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday, accusing the company of promoting Grok’s ‘spicy mode’.
The US states of Virginia and Oregon have sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX, saying the business harmed consumers by avoiding safeguards when it designed and launched an artificial intelligence chatbot capable of creating sexualised images.
The attorneys general of both states filed complaints in separate lawsuits on Monday.
Several states had announced investigations into Grok over similar claims in recent months, but Virginia and Oregon are the first states to sue.
The lawsuits filed in state courts accuse SpaceX of misleading consumers about Grok’s safety and failing to put adequate safeguards in place while promoting its “spicy mode”. The feature allows users to take an existing photograph of a person and generate a sexual or nude image or video, according to the lawsuits.
The company prioritised its business model over the safety of millions of people, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in his state’s lawsuit.
“To push its lagging product, Grok, to tens of millions of new users, it stripped out industry-standard safeguards and marketed a ‘spicy mode’ built to produce nudity,” Jones said in the lawsuit. “For these Defendants, weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature.”
Virginia and Oregon accused SpaceX of violating their respective consumer protection laws. They are seeking damages, penalties and court orders forcing the company to stop violating state law.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Grok is available to users of X, the social media platform that is a subsidiary of SpaceX.
In a statement posted on X on Monday that did not directly address the lawsuits, the platform’s safety team said it had taken action to block prompts that could generate sexualised or nude imagery and worked with law enforcement to pursue people who use the platform to make it.
“The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards,” the company posted.
Virginia’s lawsuit cites data from a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate, which estimated that between December 2025 and January 2026, Grok generated and posted millions of sexualised images on X, including more than 20,000 depicting children.
Investigators from the attorney general’s office in Virginia found that Grok’s image moderation was inconsistent, and that the bot would advise users on how to circumvent the moderation measures by avoiding words that triggered it, according to the lawsuit.
Beginning in January, Grok told users that its image generation features were only for paying subscribers, which did not stop the images’ creation but allowed the company to profit from them, the lawsuit said.
SpaceX is facing more than a dozen lawsuits brought by individuals who say nonconsensual sexual images of them as minors or adults were generated by Grok.

noticias.titulo: US drug prices leave patients facing impossible choices
noticias.resumen: Despite having jobs and health insurance, some of the US's sickest patients have trouble affording medicines they need.
noticias.texto:
US drug prices leave patients facing impossible choices
Despite working and having health insurance, some of the country’s sickest patients have trouble affording the medicines they need.
Sarah Wisniewski and her sister were once contemplating an extraordinary arrangement to manage their shared multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnoses: alternating months taking a life-changing medication.
The drug, which Wisniewski says costs thousands of dollars a month without insurance coverage, was so expensive that the sisters considered rationing their treatment rather than going without it entirely.
“It’s a weird thing to have to think about,” the 45-year-old told Al Jazeera. “You go to college, you get insurance, you get a good job, you pay your bills, you do everything right and, still, you’re having to ration your medication.”
Wisniewski is one of more than four in 10 adults in the United States who did not take medication as prescribed last year because of the cost, estimates KFF, an independent health policy research organisation.
Her experience highlights the growing financial pressures facing some of the nation’s sickest patients, who have trouble affording costly prescription medications, despite having jobs and private health insurance.
‘Every spare dime’ needed for medications
Wisniewski was diagnosed with MS in 2017 after experiencing increasingly debilitating symptoms, including difficulties with her vision, mobility and breathing.
She became one of the nearly eight in 10 American adults who are living with at least one chronic condition, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
In the summer of 2024, her neurologist prescribed Kesimpta, a medication that, she says, dramatically improved her condition. But her insurance company, Blue Cross Blue Shield, notified her it would not cover the treatment.
Wisniewski appealed three times before requesting a hearing in her state of Maryland. Only weeks before that hearing was due to take place did her insurer agree to cover the medication.
Without that intervention, Wisniewski said, she would have faced a monthly bill of approximately $10,000.
The impact of obtaining treatment has been significant on her life.
“I went from barely being able to walk … Now, I walk my dog every morning, a mile-and-a-half to two miles,” she said.
Wisniewski has also been able to maintain her federal contracting job, which she described as highly technical and demanding.
But the financial burden remains substantial. Even with the help of insurance, Wisniewski estimates she spends between $800 and $900 each month on medication.
“Almost every spare dime I get is going to just keeping me healthy, so I can make it to work the next day,” she said.
‘A uniquely American problem’
Unlike many countries, particularly wealthier ones, the US allows pharmaceutical companies significantly more latitude to set their own prices.
According to the Patients For Affordable Drugs Now patient-advocacy organisation, current laws give manufacturers “unilateral power to set launch prices in the US and the ability to raise prices at will”.
“I believe this is a uniquely American problem, ”Wisniewski said. “Other countries are … able to provide for their citizens these drugs, if not for free, at an affordable level.”
The monthly cost of her medication in Canada is 2,333 Canadian dollars ($1,623). It’s even lower in Australia at 41 Australian dollars ($27) or 6.60 Australian dollars ($4.37) with a concession card, which allows eligible residents in the country to receive discounts on healthcare and prescription medicines.
The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA), a consortium that represents US drug companies, argues that a complicated network of third-party middlemen, known as pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), and insurance companies are to blame for the country’s high drug prices.
“PBMs and insurers control benefits through processes like prior authorisation, embedded step therapy, and formulary controls that may allow PBMs and insurers to deny coverage or push patients to alternative treatments from the initially prescribed medicine,” PhRMA’s website said. The organisation did not reply to a request for comment.
A study by the nonpartisan RAND organisation, released in 2024, found that US prescription drug prices were substantially higher than those in other wealthy countries, particularly for name-brand medications.
Using 2022 data, RAND’s researchers found that US manufacturers’ gross prices across all prescription drugs were 278 percent higher than the average prices in 33 other high-income countries. For brand-name drugs, US prices were more than four times the comparison-country average.
But the consequences of the current US system can extend far beyond the cost of individual prescriptions.
Wisniewski said the money she spends maintaining access to medication is money she cannot put toward local businesses, transportation or investments in her community.
“I really think that a lot of people, at an abstract level, understand that this could happen to anybody at any point in time,” she said. “But I don’t think that it really hits home to folks that you are legitimately one bad phone call away from losing everything.”
What can be done?
After this month’s historic midterm elections in the US, where Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress by wide margins, there will be few areas of agreement with Democrats’ Republican counterparts – and President Donald Trump.
But targeted reforms that address the high cost of prescriptions could be an area where both parties find common ground.
A survey conducted by Fabrizio Ward in March 2025 found more than three in four voters – including 70 percent of Trump supporters – wanted Congress to take action on reducing drug prices.
The issue was the focus of a US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday of last week, when lawmakers and healthcare experts examined how pharmaceutical companies and insurers influence pricing and access to medication.
At that November 17 hearing, witnesses highlighted several factors contributing to high prescription drug costs, including pharmaceutical patent protections and the role of PBMs.
Merith Basey, chief executive officer of Patients For Affordable Drugs Now, argued that pharmaceutical companies exploit the patent system to delay competition from cheaper alternatives.
One of those practices, known as patent thicketing, involves companies securing multiple patents covering different aspects of a medication or its delivery device, potentially making it more difficult for competitors to introduce generic alternatives.
Basey told lawmakers the introduction of generic competition could substantially reduce prices, arguing a single generic competitor can lower a drug’s price by 39 percent, while six or more competitors can reduce prices by as much as 95 percent.
But other witnesses pointed to PBMs, claiming their involvement in distributing drugs can influence pricing.
The Senate panel has advanced a number of proposals to tackle the high cost of prescription drugs in the US. One of those is the bipartisan Eliminating Thickets to Improve Competition (ETHIC) Act, which would limit the practice of patent thickening, making it easier for generic drugs to enter the US market and lower costs.
“Big Pharma knows exactly what it’s doing in monopolising the US patent system: driving up drug costs for Americans while preventing generic-drug manufacturers from getting their foot in the market,” Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, one of the bill’s sponsors, said in a statement.
Wisniewski noted that while the ETHIC Act wouldn’t make her prescription “cheap”, it would be “astronomically better than what we have now”.

noticias.titulo: Iran flogs singer Parastoo Ahmadi for performing without headscarf
noticias.resumen: Ahmadi and four production team members also face two-year bans on travel and artistic activity.
noticias.texto:
Iran flogs singer Parastoo Ahmadi for performing without headscarf
Ahmadi and four production team members also face two-year bans on travel and artistic activity.
Iran has flogged a singer and her production team after they were convicted of “offending public decency”, according to local media.
The sentence of 74 lashes handed down to Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her team was carried out in the city of Qom on Monday, the singer’s lawyer Mostafa Nili told the Emtedad news website.
A court in the city had sentenced the quintet in June. They were convicted of “producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online” over a video showing Ahmadi performing without wearing the mandatory hijab alongside male musicians.
The video was posted on YouTube in December 2024. In addition to the flogging, the five were banned for two years from taking part in artistic and musical activities and leaving Iran.
Western governments and human rights groups have condemned flogging as a form of torture that violates international law.
Iran rejects criticism of its human rights record and says Western countries should address abuses of their own.
Iran’s mandatory hijab rules became a focal point of protests in 2022 after Mahsa Amini, a Kurdish Iranian woman, died in custody following her arrest for allegedly violating the dress code.
More women have since defied the rules in Tehran and elsewhere in Iran, while authorities have enforced them more selectively.

Inside Story
Iran hits US bases and civilian sites in the Gulf after a lull
Tehran has ramped up attacks in recent days as the US naval blockade and sanctions campaign hurt the country.
After a relative lull in its conflict with the United States, Iran is striking US assets in Gulf countries again. Civilian facilities have been damaged.
Is Iran just tightening its grip on the global economy?
Can Tehran force the White House to ease its economic blockade?
And could this revive a full-scale conflict?
Presenter: Rob Matheson

Ali Akbar Dareini — Researcher at the Center for Strategic Studies

noticias.titulo: Turkish police hunting for lioness stalking Istanbul
noticias.resumen: Questions being asked about big cat's origins, with suspicion falling on the country's growing role in animal smuggling.
noticias.texto:
Turkish police hunting for lioness stalking Istanbul
Questions are being asked about how the big cat arrived, with suspicion falling on the country’s growing role as a hub for wild-animal smuggling.
Police and animal welfare teams have launched a hunt for a lioness reported to be prowling the outskirts of Istanbul.
City authorities closed a woodland area in the northern Sariyer district on Monday as the teams expanded a search for the big cat, which was spotted in the area the previous evening.
Turkiye’s National Parks Directorate said on Sunday that police officers in Zekeriyakoy, north of Istanbul’s European side, had reported spotting “an animal resembling a lion” on surveillance cameras.
Grainy security camera footage republished by Turkish media appeared to show what looked like a big cat prowling across a patch of open countryside.
Istanbul Governor Davut Gul’s office confirmed the information, saying that “the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive”.
The parks authority said specialist veterinarians and teams equipped with thermal imaging cameras were assisting in the search.
More than 70 personnel, supported by drones, were searching in and around the nearby Belgrade Forest, which covers 54 square kilometres (21 square miles) north of Istanbul.
Local resident Arda Koc said he saw the lioness after joining the search on Sunday evening.
“I took my car and went out for a drive hoping to see it,” he told Turkiye’s Cumhuriyet newspaper. “While I was driving, it suddenly jumped out in front of me. At first I was scared. After that, I immediately notified the gendarmerie.”
Residents have been warned of the danger, and police were stationed on roads leading into and out of the neighbourhood.
Sariyer District Mayor Mustafa Oktay Aksu noted that the lioness had not harmed chickens she passed at night, indicating she had been hand-reared. However, he warned that she should still be treated as dangerous.
Meanwhile, activists and professors have questioned how the species was brought into Turkiye.
Doganay Tolunay, a professor in the forestry department of Istanbul University-Cerrahpasa, said on X on Monday that questions that need to be asked should include “how a globally threatened species was brought into our country, how it got through customs, why those feeding it have yet to be identified” and “what will happen if the lion is caught”.
Turkiye has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.
In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.

Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia chief: How did we get here?

noticias.titulo: Protesting Bangladesh garment workers reject pay offer
noticias.resumen: Bangladesh’s garment industry brings in about $38bn a year. The minimum wage is around 12,500 taka ($100) per month.
noticias.texto:
Protesting Bangladesh garment workers reject pay offer
Bangladesh’s garment industry brings in about $38bn a year. The minimum wage is around 12,500 taka ($100) per month.
Representatives of Bangladeshi garment workers have rejected a pay offer from employers.
Factory owners submitted a pay proposal at a meeting convened by the government-appointed wage board on Monday, but worker representatives dismissed it as too low.
The failure to reach an agreement during the wage talks suggests that the weeks of strikes and protests over the minimum wage in the industry could persist.
Babul Akhter, who represents workers on the wage board, told reporters after the meeting that “the offer … falls far short of what we have been demanding”, according to the AFP news agency.
The board kept the figure that had been offered confidential, although Chairman Judge Syed Azad Subhani said the proposed monthly minimum wage was above 14,500 taka ($116).
Workers’ representatives had formally proposed 32,000 taka ($258) for the lowest regular pay grade and 30,000 taka ($241) for apprentices.
Bangladesh’s garment industry brings in about $38bn a year, employs around four million people, and accounts for roughly four-fifths of the country’s export earnings.
However, the world’s second-largest garment exporter after China has seen widespread protests since October. Strikes have disrupted production at factories across the country, closing around 500 of its more than 4,000 clothing factories.
Workers say that wages have failed to keep up with the rising cost of food, housing, transport and healthcare.
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association estimated that 317 factories lost $428m in production between November 1 and 18.
During the last wage review in 2023, labour groups rallied for a monthly minimum of at least 23,000 taka ($185). The government set it at 12,500 taka ($100), a figure unions rejected at the time but ultimately accepted.
They are now pushing for an increase of around 140 percent, but their anger has risen due to the closure of around 500 plants by employers.
A “no work, no pay” provision in the country’s labour laws allows factory owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.

noticias.titulo: Trump delays explosive detonation in US state of Iowa amid legal battles
noticias.resumen: Iowa detonation postponed as Trump cites safety risks, lead exposure, and court rulings in Midwestern controversy.
noticias.texto:
Trump delays explosive detonation in US state of Iowa amid legal battles
Iowa detonation postponed as Trump cites safety risks, lead exposure, and court rulings in Midwestern controversy.
United States President Donald Trump has ordered the military to delay a planned controlled detonation of more than four tonnes of explosives in the Midwestern state of Iowa until a federal appeals court and the state’s governor sign off on it.
Trump’s announcement on Monday comes amid a string of delays and a late-stage legal challenge raised by environmental groups in Iowa over approximately 9,700 pounds of degraded lead azide stored in 68 drums at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near the city of Middletown.
“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this long-term problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” the president posted on his Truth Social platform.
Inside the legal fight to halt the blasts
The explosions — originally set to take place on Friday before being postponed until Monday — first hit a legal obstacle after environmental health advocacy groups, the Sierra Club and the Iowa Environmental Council, filed a petition for review and an emergency motion seeking to halt the detonation on Thursday.
They questioned the legality of an emergency permit the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted on November 13, which authorised the military to move forward with the blasts under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA).
The plaintiffs pointed out that nearby residents were only given a week’s notice and that the blasts could send lead dust as far as 160km (100 miles).
They also argued that the EPA failed to properly assess safer disposal methods.
In response to the suit, the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit temporarily froze the EPA’s emergency detonation permit last week while it reviewed the case.
But in a November 21 court filing, the Justice Department maintained that the army could still proceed with the two controlled blasts under an emergency exemption.
Trump warns of ‘death or destruction’
In his Monday post, the president blamed the Obama administration for improperly storing the munitions in 2009.
Military officials have previously noted the barrels were kept at the Iowa facility — in a mixture of water and ethanol — for more than two decades.
According to a court declaration, an Army munitions expert found that the liquid in the drums had evaporated, causing needle-shaped crystals to form as recently as March.
The president also warned that blocking the destruction of the unstable explosive carries dire consequences — and that incoming Democratic Senator Rob Sand would be responsible should the material spontaneously detonate.
Sand, who previously criticised an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity” around the blast, has warned that blowing up the stockpile could send a toxic plume of lead dust across communities in southeastern Iowa and neighbouring Illinois. Lead is a dense metal associated with severe health risks, including birth defects.
Sand’s office did not respond to questions.
Trump further emphasised that current weather conditions are optimal for a controlled blast and framed any further delay as a choice by the courts and Iowa’s incoming leadership.
“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and long-term, situation,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

noticias.titulo: US adds Megaspeed, at center of Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist
noticias.resumen: The Trump administration has added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist after tensions over its failure to do so raised questions. The news came the same day that Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO.
noticias.texto:
US adds Megaspeed, at center of Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist
November 23, 2026
The Trump administration added Megaspeed International, the firm at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist on Monday.
That means that the Singapore-based firm will not be able to obtain US technology, including semiconductors, without obtaining a license from the US government.
The news was reported by Semafor, an American news website.
US Commerce Department under scrutiny over Nvidia scandal: What to know
The US Commerce Department had been investigating whether Megaspeed was smuggling Nvidia chips into China for more than a year, according to the Financial Times.
But tensions at the Commerce Department broke into the spotlight after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with an executive at the Singapore-based firm earlier this month.
Politicians criticized Commerce Department Secretary Howard Lutnick for not having previously added Megaspeed to the department's so-called "Entity List" despite US intelligence warnings that the company was a possible front for smuggling sensitive AI chip technology to China.
Huang briefly lost his job over the scandal as US officials said the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday, in a stunning reversal after his resignation just two weeks ago.
The New York Times reported last month that US authorities had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with Jensen Huang.
Beijing has denied those claims and called the spy accusations "groundless."
Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
Nvidia shares soared more than 30% after the company announced it reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
Some people were happy to see him back as president of Nvidia, as videos posted to social media show.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is on track to be the next speaker of the House, called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible, and incomprehensible" and vowed Congress would reinvestigate any wrongdoing by the company and the Commerce Department.

noticias.titulo: Denmark: Top court backs hardline immigration "ghetto law"
noticias.resumen: Denmark's Supreme Court has found that evictions of "non-Western" residents do not amount to discrimination. The government in Copenhagen argues its "ghetto law" encourages integration.
noticias.texto:
Denmark: Top court backs hardline law against 'non-Westerners'
November 23, 2026
Denmark's Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a housing association that terminated 91 leases in order to prevent the label "hard ghetto" being applied to their housing complex. The decision align's with Copenhagen's hardline approach to immigration.
The court on Monday upheld Denmark's 2018 "ghetto law," which allows for the relocation of "non-Western" residents from minority-heavy neighborhoods in order to foster integration. The Danish court ruling diverges from a top EU court decision last year that found application of the law could amount to discrimination.
The Danish laws requires social housing estates to rebuild, renovate and adjust their social mix if these become minority heavy, stipulating that 60% of apartments be rented to "Westerners" at market value by 2030.
Denmark's hardline immigration policies making it a role model in the EU
Denmark's pioneering role in spearheading tougher immigration rules has made it a model for some in the EU. Denmark was also one of five countries that last week announced its intent to set up an asylum seeker deportation hub in Rwanda.
Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed Monday's decision, saying it "strengthens security, social cohesion and integration."
The court's decision upheld a 2022 lower court ruling against seven tenants who fought their evictions in Nojsomhed, Helsingor, just north of Copenhagen.
In Monday's ruling, the law was found to be non-discriminatory when it comes to the eviction of "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries" as it is not broadly based on ethnicity. The EU ruling focused on this particular aspect, saying the law would be discriminatory if criteria were race based, while ultimately allowing national courts to have the last say in the matter.
"The Supreme Court notes that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups [immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons]. Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups," read the Danish court's ruling.
Who is a 'non-Western' resident?
Tenants' associations estimate that 11,000 people across Denmark will have to be relocated to comply with the law.
The housing association in question issued a written statement saying that it was aware that the evictions would impact those affected, adding that it undertook measures to insure that residents found new homes.
According to Statistics Denmark's definition, "non-Western" countries include every country other than the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Australia, Britain, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the United States and the Vatican.

noticias.titulo: Tajikistan follows US call, withdraws from ICC
noticias.resumen: Tajikistan has initiated its withdrawal from the International Criminal Court as the US calls for it to be "dismantled." The decision was made during a recent visit from Russian President Vladimir Putin.
noticias.texto:
Tajikistan withdraws from ICC, follows US call
November 23, 2026
Tajikistan has now become the fourth country to announce its formal withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague, Netherlands since the US announced its intention to "dismantle" the body — joining Chad, Naoero [formerly Nauru] and Venezuela.
US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have railed against the court as abusing its jurisdiction, with Trump publicly attacking the ICC during remarks at a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin — who is wanted by the court for war crimes committed during the course of Russia's full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
Trump's public attacks on the world's permanent war crimes tribunal prompted an amused smirk from Putin during their meeting in Shenzhen, China.
Why is the ICC important?
The ICC prosecutes individuals accused of genocide, crimes against humanity, crimes of aggression and war crimes in instances when national cannot or will not act.
The ICC issued an international arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023.
Tajikistan's government said it made the decision to initiate the one-year withdrawal process on Friday, when Putin made a stopover visit after leaving his trilateral meeting with Trump and Xi.
The ICC said it "regrets" Tajikistan's decision, adding that the move undermines "the collective pursuit of justice" and weakens "global efforts to end impunity."
"The ICC stands at the heart of the international system of accountability, and its effectiveness depends on sustained and unequivocal support from the international community," an ICC statement continued.
Tajikistan signed the Rome Statute that established the ICC back in 1998 and ratified it in 2000.
Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have also announced their withdrawal from the court, blasting it as a tool of "neocolonial repression."

noticias.titulo: North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate
noticias.resumen: EU enlargement has regained momentum, with Montenegro and Albania moving closer to membership. But North Macedonia, a candidate since 2005, remains stalled by a politically difficult dispute involving Bulgaria.
noticias.texto:
North Macedonia watches as EU enlargement moves on
November 23, 2026
The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.
But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.
That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.
"The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa said ahead of the meeting.
Prepared, but the handbrake is still on
North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards.
But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Plan.
However, she added, "the handbrake on its accession negotiations is still on."
Kos said that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022.
What's blocking N. Macedonia's EU progress?
The stalemate has deep roots.
For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path.
Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow.
Bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities.
The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable.
'Not blocked by a member state'
From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework.
"It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast.
North Macedonia's government sees the problem differently.
EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia.
Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history: Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people.
President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another.
"We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she said.
Strong support for membership, little appetite for compromise
After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia.
A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%.
Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession currently required to move forward.
That, he says, helps preserve the status quo.
High domestic political stakes
The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat.
The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions.
For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks.
The EU, meanwhile, is not offering to reopen the negotiating framework.
The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal.
According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise.
"If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.

noticias.titulo: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
noticias.resumen: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.
noticias.texto:
Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
November 23, 2026
Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."
In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.
"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.
Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.
Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.
Ramping up electricity production
As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.
In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.
While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.
"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."
Drilling for oil
At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.
Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.
The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.
Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.
"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."
The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.
"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."
Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.
Carbon trading 'breakthrough?'
Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."
Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.
"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.
Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.
"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.
"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."
This interview also appeared as a video.

noticias.titulo: California Democrat Rep. Gomez resigns following ethics report on sexual misconduct allegations
noticias.resumen: California Congressman Rep. Jimmy Gomez says he will resign after a House Ethics report concluded Gomez's actions violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances."
noticias.texto:
California Democrat Rep. Gomez resigns following ethics report on sexual misconduct allegations
Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., says he is resigning from Congress after a bipartisan investigation released Monday found "substantial evidence" he engaged in sexual misconduct toward a House staffer.
The House Ethics Committee concluded Gomez violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances and engaging in unwelcome sexual conduct towards a House staffer and disregarding the power imbalance inherent in his relationship with House staffers."
The report also says the behavior could constitute criminal sexual assault.
Gomez has served in Congress since 2017 representing parts of Los Angeles. He lost reelection this fall to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres. California uses a system where the top two vote-getters no matter the party advance to the general election. Gomez says his resignation will be effective Dec. 1.
Lisa Banks and Sarah Nesbitt, attorneys for the unnamed House staffer, wrote in a statement that their client testified to the committee truthfully and at personal risk.
"She sacrificed her own sense of safety and privacy to help reveal the ongoing misogyny and debauchery that permeates Capitol Hill," Banks and Nesbitt wrote. "Representative Gomez seems to believe that the power he wields, both as a man and as a member of Congress, makes him untouchable. Today's findings are a meaningful step toward dismantling that belief."
In a statement announcing his plan to resign, Gomez wrote that he cooperated with the investigation, but has strong disagreements with the report and its conclusions.
"Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred," he wrote.
"I also have serious concerns about the process. In my interview, I answered the Committee's questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond."
The House Ethics Committee, which includes five Democrats and five Republicans, opened its investigation into Gomez in August following a press report of Gomez kissing a staffer from another Congressional office at a party. Gomez denied those allegations.
The committee asked Gomez to disclose whether he "ever engaged in a romantic or sexual relationship or made sexual contact with a congressional staffer." Gomez disclosed interactions with two women — telling the committee the encounters were all consensual. Both women spoke to the committee.
One denied "she had ever had a nonconsensual sexual encounter" with Gomez. The other, described as Witness 1 in the report, said she had more than one encounter with Gomez and she did not consider them consensual.
She told investigators that Gomez made sexual contact without her consent at a bar in February 2024 and then was forceful with her and tried to kiss her at his congressional office in July 2024.
Gomez denied the interactions were nonconsensual. The staffer, described as Witness 1 in the committee report, eventually left her job on Capitol Hill.
"Here, the House lost Witness 1 as a competent and able staffer because of Representative Gomez's misconduct and because of a broader culture of disrespect and toxic sexual behavior toward staff that permeates life on the Hill and is long overdue for correction," the committee wrote.
The report comes amid a broader conversation about how Congress deals with the behavior of its members, especially when it comes to sexual misconduct.
In April, Democrat Eric Swalwell of California resigned his House seat amid allegations of sexual assault and misconduct. He also denied the allegations. Rep. Tony Gonzales (R-Tex.) also resigned from the House after admitting to an affair with a former staff member.
Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) dropped his reelection bid earlier this year after the House Ethics Committee recommended he face a censure vote for allegedly harassing two young female staffers. Edwards denied the allegations.
Republican Reps. Max Miller of Ohio and Cory Mills of Florida also face House Ethics investigations stemming from allegations of domestic violence. Both deny wrongdoing.
Miller lost his reelection bid this fall and Mills lost his GOP primary.
Last week, the House Ethics Committee adopted new rules with the aim of speeding up investigations into sexual misconduct and improving transparency.

Mending relationships over the holidays? Considering a truce? NPR wants to know
